COMMON LAW MARRIAGE IN CALIFORNIA — NON-RECOGNITION INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Morgan Casey Lee

DECLARATION OF PARTIES AND PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This Common Law Marriage in California — Non-Recognition Information Sheet concerns Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee. It describes what California law says, in general terms, about two related subjects: (1) the requirements California itself imposes to form a marriage within the state, and why living together and presenting oneself as married does not, by itself, create a marriage here; and (2) the separate rule under which California courts will generally recognize a marriage — including one formed under another jurisdiction's common law marriage doctrine — that was validly contracted under the law of the jurisdiction where it was formed. This information sheet states general legal facts. It does not determine, and takes no position on, whether Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Casey Lee are or are not married under the law of California or any other jurisdiction; that determination depends on the specific facts of their relationship and history and, if disputed, is for a court to decide.

CALIFORNIA'S OWN REQUIREMENTS FOR FORMING A MARRIAGE
California statute defines marriage as "a personal relation arising out of a civil contract between two persons, to which the consent of the parties capable of making that contract is necessary," but the statute is explicit that the parties' mutual consent to be married is not, by itself, enough. Consent must be followed by the issuance of a marriage license and solemnization of the marriage as authorized by the Family Code, subject to two named statutory exceptions: Section 425 (which concerns marriage by a party who is confined or physically incapacitated) and Part 4 of the same division, commencing with Section 500 (which concerns the state's confidential-marriage license track). Outside those two exceptions, a couple in California must obtain a license and have the marriage solemnized for a marriage to be formed; consent and cohabitation alone do not suffice.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Consent alone does not constitute marriage. Consent must be followed by the issuance of a license and solemnization as authorized by this division, except as provided by Section 425 and Part 4 (commencing with Section 500)."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 300(a) (California Legislative Information text), consent alone insufficient; license and solemnization required, subject to two named exceptions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=300.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes and summarizes Family Code section 300(a) only; it does not independently verify the text of Section 425 or of Part 4 (commencing with Section 500), the two exceptions the statute itself names, beyond quoting that they are named exceptions. It does not quote or summarize subsection (b) of Section 300, which addresses when a license becomes a marriage certificate, because that subsection is not relevant to this topic. No case law was independently verified for this clause; California case law construing and applying Section 300 was not fetched or reviewed in the course of preparing this document, so this clause rests on the current statutory text alone, fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website. This document is informational only: it does not itself determine whether any specific couple has satisfied, or failed to satisfy, these requirements.

NO MARRIAGE IS FORMED WITHIN CALIFORNIA BY COHABITATION ALONE
Because California's own marriage-formation statute requires a license and solemnization — and expressly states that the parties' consent by itself does not constitute a marriage — no marriage is formed within California merely because two people live together and present themselves to others as a married couple, no matter how long that arrangement continues. This is sometimes described as California not recognizing "common law marriage" formed within the state. The absence of a license and solemnization is not cured by any particular length of cohabitation, by the couple's own description of themselves as married, by filing joint tax returns, by sharing a residence or finances, or by using a shared surname.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Consent alone does not constitute marriage."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 300(a) (California Legislative Information text), consent alone does not constitute a marriage (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=300.)
  Known gap: This clause is this document's own inference from the plain text of Family Code section 300(a) — the same statutory text quoted in this document's companion clause on California's formation requirements — rather than a quotation from a case holding that specific proposition. A substantial body of California case law is understood to confirm that California does not recognize common law marriage formed within the state, but no such case was independently fetched or verified in the course of preparing this document: CourtListener searches were attempted (queries for "common law marriage California recognition" and related terms, run against California courts and generally), but the CourtListener API's daily request quota was exhausted before any candidate opinion's actual text could be fetched and confirmed, so no case citation is included here. This document is informational only and does not itself determine any specific couple's marital status.

CALIFORNIA'S RECOGNITION OF A MARRIAGE VALIDLY CONTRACTED ELSEWHERE
A separate California statute addresses marriages formed outside California: "A marriage contracted outside this state that would be valid by laws of the jurisdiction in which the marriage was contracted is valid in California." This rule is not limited to marriages formed by license and ceremony elsewhere; on its face it extends to any marriage — including one formed under another jurisdiction's common law marriage doctrine, where that jurisdiction recognizes such marriages — that was validly contracted under the law of the place where it was formed. California courts generally give this kind of recognition to an out-of-state marriage.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A marriage contracted outside this state that would be valid by laws of the jurisdiction in which the marriage was contracted is valid in California."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 308 (California Legislative Information text), a marriage valid where contracted is valid in California (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=308.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes and summarizes Family Code section 308 in isolation; it does not independently verify any other Family Code section that might qualify or limit this general rule (for example, statutory exceptions for marriages entered into in violation of another state's own laws, or marriages this state might refuse to recognize as against a strong California public policy). No case law was independently verified for this clause: CourtListener searches were attempted, but the API's daily request quota was exhausted before any candidate opinion applying Section 308 (or its predecessor rule) to a common law marriage could be fetched and confirmed, so this clause rests on the current statutory text alone, fetched directly from the California Legislative Information website. This document does not itself determine that any specific marriage was, or was not, validly contracted under the law of any other jurisdiction.

RECOGNITION DEPENDS ON ACTUAL VALIDITY UNDER THE OTHER JURISDICTION'S OWN LAW
The California statute recognizing an out-of-state marriage measures validity "by laws of the jurisdiction in which the marriage was contracted" — not by California law, and not by the couple's own description of their relationship. A jurisdiction that recognizes common law marriage typically imposes its own set of requirements before treating a couple as married without a license or ceremony — requirements that commonly include matters such as the couple's capacity to marry, their mutual and present agreement to be married, cohabitation, holding themselves out as married, and, in a number of states that recognize common law marriage, that the couple be domiciled in that state at the relevant time. These requirements vary by jurisdiction and are set by each jurisdiction's own law, not by California's Family Code. Under the statute's own terms, a couple's travel through, vacation in, or temporary presence in a jurisdiction that recognizes common law marriage does not by itself establish that a marriage was contracted there.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "valid by laws of the jurisdiction in which the marriage was contracted"
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 308 (California Legislative Information text), validity measured by the law of the jurisdiction where the marriage was contracted (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=308.)
  Known gap: The specific common law marriage requirements of any other state (which states recognize it at all, and each one's own elements such as a domicile requirement) are not addressed by California's Family Code and were not independently researched or verified against any other state's statutes or case law in the course of preparing this document; this clause describes, in general terms, how the California statute's own "valid by laws of the jurisdiction in which the marriage was contracted" language directs the inquiry to that other jurisdiction's law, without asserting the specific content of any other state's law. No California case law applying this principle to a specific common law marriage was independently verified for this clause: CourtListener searches were attempted, but the API's daily request quota was exhausted before any candidate opinion's text could be fetched and confirmed. This document does not itself determine whether any specific couple met any other jurisdiction's common law marriage requirements, or was domiciled in any other jurisdiction at any particular time.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT — NOT A COURT FILING
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct to the best of my knowledge.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.
